title: The City That Rose to Meet Him
story:
News traveled ahead of the chariots. Krishna was coming — not for a visit this time, but for the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice through which Yudhishthira, king of the Pandavas at Indraprastha, meant to be acknowledged as a king of kings. And the city of Indraprastha met him the way a festival meets the sun.

The streets had been swept and sprinkled with water fragrant with elephant musk. Banners streamed from every rooftop, golden arches stood at the crossings, and at each doorway stood the full pitchers of water that are the old sign of welcome. From the palace Yudhishthira came out to meet him with his teachers and his friends, and the sound that went before them was music and the chanting of the Vedas together. When Krishna stepped down, the heart of the king of the Pandavas melted. Yudhishthira took him in both arms and held him, and the embrace said everything a court could not.

Bhima embraced him next, smiling through eyes blurred with love — Krishna was his mother's sister's son, his own cousin. Arjuna folded him in his arms. The twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, bowed and touched his feet. Around them the bards and the heralds sang his praises, and the whole assembly seemed to press inward, each person wanting to be nearer to him. Of that welcome the old telling says simply that Krishna stood at its center like the jewel crowning a hundred good names.

The women of the city had dropped their household work the moment the news came. Down the king's road they hurried, hair-braids coming loose and garments slipping in their eagerness, to stand where they could watch him pass, and from the rooftops they showered him with flowers, welcoming him with smiles, embracing him in their hearts. Those who caught sight of Krishna's queens — Rukmini, Satyabhama, Bhadra, Jambavati — murmured to one another that the ladies of the Vrishni house moved among them like the stars around the moon. What had those women done, they asked, to be looked on by one whose glance made a festival of the eyes of all the world?

In the palace, Kunti rose from her couch and went to meet her sister's son. Krishna bowed to his aunt and to the elder women of the household, and Kunti led him into the house with her own hands. At her mother-in-law's bidding, Draupadi welcomed each of Krishna's queens — Kalindi, Mitravinda, Saibya, Nagnajiti, and the rest — and settled them in the women's quarters with every honor.

Yudhishthira gave Krishna the best of the palace, and when Krishna was seated at ease, the king spoke. In the Mahabharata's telling his words are plain. "It is because of you that the whole earth is under my rule," he said. "Through your grace I have gathered this wealth, and I wish to give it away as the rites ordain — to the brahmin priests and to the sacred fire. Grant me leave to perform the sacrifice with you and my brothers. Better still, take your own place at the head of it, for if you perform it, I shall be cleansed of every sin."

Krishna answered with the affection of a friend who wants nothing from the friendship. "You deserve imperial dignity. Let the great sacrifice be performed by you; if you perform it and gain its fruit, we will all count ourselves crowned with success. I am always seeking your good. Perform the sacrifice you desire — and give me some office in it, for I should obey all your commands."

"Then my resolve is already crowned with fruit," Yudhishthira said, "since you have come just as I wished."

So the son of Pandu set himself, with his brothers, to gathering everything the Rajasuya would need, and an arrival of embraces and showers of flowers became the beginning of the greatest sacrifice the age would see. For a few days more, though, there was only this: a king's city gladdened by the presence of its truest friend, like a dark region made bright by the sun.
reflection: The Rajasuya is often remembered as the summit of Yudhishthira's glory, but this story records the arrival as pure affection — a city that empties its households to see one man pass. The political begins as the personal: the king who would conquer the world first asks his cousin to bless the undertaking.
tradition_note: The Mahabharata frames the same arrival differently — Krishna coming with a mass of treasure for Yudhishthira and a Yadava army under Vasudeva's command. This account follows the Bhagavata's framing of the arrival as a reunion of love.
next_story_tease: Yet not long before this day of glory, the same friendship had nearly been broken by an elopement — Arjuna had carried off Krishna's sister from the very heart of Dwaraka.
hero_scene: Krishna stepping down from his chariot into the flower-strewn king's road of Indraprastha, Yudhishthira embracing him with both arms while Bhima, Arjuna and the twins press close, banners and golden arches overhead and women showering flowers from the rooftops.
